nameStory: The name 'fumewort' comes from the smoky, almost ethereal appearance of the delicate flowers that seem to drift like wisps of colored smoke above the foliage. 'Incised' refers to the deeply cut, finely divided leaves that look like they've been carefully carved with tiny scissors. This delicate wildflower gets its scientific name Corydalis from the Greek word for 'crested lark,' as the spurred flowers reminded botanists of a lark's head crest.
description: Incised fumewort is a delicate annual or biennial wildflower that typically grows 6-12 inches tall with an airy, graceful appearance. The plant produces clusters of small, tubular flowers in shades of pink, purple, or white, each with a distinctive backward-pointing spur that gives them an almost bird-like profile. Its leaves are finely divided and feathery, creating a soft, lacy texture that complements the dainty flowers. Originally from East Asia, this charming wildflower is quite rare in New England, making any sighting a special discovery.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular flowers with a prominent backward-pointing spur, arranged in loose clusters. Flowers are typically pink, purple, or white and feel papery to the touch when mature. Each flower is bilaterally symmetrical and resembles a tiny bird's head.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, feathery leaves that feel soft and delicate between your fingers. The leaf segments are narrow and finely cut, creating a lacy, almost fern-like appearance that's very distinctive.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual or biennial herb, typically 6-12 inches tall with a branching, somewhat sprawling habit. The stems are smooth and hollow, feeling tender and easily breakable.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, elongated seed pods that develop after flowering. The pods are smooth and contain several small, dark seeds that rattle slightly when shaken when fully mature.

habitat: In its native range, incised fumewort grows in forests, clearings, and along irrigation channels, preferring somewhat disturbed soils. In New England, this extremely rare plant would most likely be found in similar semi-shaded locations with moist, well-draining soil, possibly as an escape from cultivation or botanical gardens. Look for it in woodland edges, near streams, or in cultivated areas where it might have been intentionally planted.

seasonality.spring: Begins flowering in late spring with delicate clusters of spurred flowers appearing on young plants. New growth emerges with fresh, bright green feathery foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with full flower displays and active seed production. Plants may continue flowering throughout much of summer if conditions remain favorable.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and release seeds, while annual plants begin to decline. Biennial plants may maintain some basal foliage through early fall.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, while biennial plants may persist as small rosettes under snow cover in protected locations.

funFact: This delicate wildflower is so rare in New England that it's been spotted fewer than 10 times, making it rarer than finding a four-leaf clover in your backyard - in fact, you're statistically more likely to spot several four-leaf clovers than to encounter this elusive Asian beauty in the wild!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other members of the Corydalis family, but incised fumewort's extremely finely divided, lacy leaves are more delicate than most relatives. Remember: 'incised and precise' - the leaf cuts are so fine and detailed they look like botanical artwork.
contextualKnowledge: Some botanical authorities place Corydalis in the Fumariaceae (fumitory) family rather than Papaveraceae (poppy family), reflecting ongoing scientific debate about plant relationships. The alternative common names 'purple keman' and 'murasa-kike-man' reflect its Japanese origins, where it's more commonly encountered in the wild.
compareHints: Unlike the more robust Yellow Corydalis with its coarser leaves and bright yellow flowers, incised fumewort has much more finely divided, delicate foliage and typically produces pink to purple blooms. It's also generally smaller and more delicate than Golden Corydalis, with a more refined, almost ethereal appearance. The leaf dissection in incised fumewort is among the finest in the genus, earning its 'incised' name.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bird-in-a-bush differs from other New England Corydalis species mainly in its spring ephemeral nature and tuberous root system.
Golden corydalis is quite rare in New England compared to its relatives, with only 8 recorded observations.
Yellow Corydalis differs from its corydalis cousins by its bright yellow flower color - most other corydalis species in our region have pink, purple, or white flowers.
Noble Corydalis stands out from other New England corydalis species by its larger size, bright golden-yellow flowers (rather than pink, purple, or pale yellow), and more robust growth habit.
Hollowroot differs from other New England corydalis species primarily in its early blooming time and the distinctive hollow tuber (though you shouldn't dig to check this).
Among the Corydalis species, Fern-leaved Corydalis stands out for having the most finely-divided, fern-like foliage - other corydalis have more substantial, less delicate leaves.
